objects.name: Predatory Raids
objects.description: Aggressors may organize armed attacks on the settlements of an Indigenous people for the purpose of looting, seizing material valuables, driving off livestock, and taking civilians captive. This practice depletes the demographic and economic potential of the colonized society, deprives people of the resources needed for survival, and creates a zone of constant physical threat around the metropole's installations.

objects.name: Slave Trade
objects.description: Aggressors, or the governors they appoint, may carry out the commercial sale of members of a forcibly subjugated Indigenous people into slavery. This practice is used both for the direct illegal enrichment of the occupation apparatus and for the physical depletion of the colonized society's demographic potential through the permanent removal and export of people beyond the lands of their historical residence.

objects.name: Comprehensive Reconnaissance of Territories
objects.description: Aggressors deliberately organize the collection of strategic, geographic, demographic, and economic data on target territories. Within this technique, the colonizer sends diplomats, merchants, explorers, or specialized expeditions to determine the population size of a potential object of colonization, assess its defensive capacity and infrastructure, and survey mineral deposits and natural resources. The information obtained is used by the metropole to plan a subsequent seizure by force, the establishment of control, or economic exploitation. The colonizer's emissaries often attempt to win over the population with gifts it values (for example, glass beads resembling objects used as money and perceived as foreign currency) or through mutually beneficial trade exchange. In some cases, people are drawn into participation in rituals that the colonizer later construes as a declaration of allegiance.

objects.name: Imposition of Alien Governance
objects.description: The occupation administration artificially deprives subordinated societies of the right to self-governance, appointing loyal representatives of foreign elites over them. Unlike the creation of puppet governments (T0037), this technique does not aim to simulate a civil conflict or to create the appearance of a legitimate local authority. The use of alien overseers is employed by the metropole for open domination, the destruction of the Indigenous people's traditional social ties, and the uninterrupted mobilization of resources.

objects.name: Pitting Neighboring Peoples Against Each Other
objects.description: The metropole deliberately sows and sustains enmity between neighboring Indigenous peoples so that they weaken one another and do not unite against it. Instead of confronting a united resistance, the colonizer divides it: it sets one people against another, arms and rewards the loyal against the defiant, and converts the shared hostility toward the empire into mutual discord among those being subjugated. The mechanism relies on already existing or artificially inflamed differences — clan-based, territorial, confessional — and entrenches them as a permanent line of division, depriving Indigenous peoples of the ability to act together. The metropole meanwhile preserves its own troops, shifting part of the suppression onto the incited side and presenting itself as an arbiter.

objects.name: Creation of Puppet Religious Institutions
objects.description: Aggressors may establish their own fully controlled religious posts and structures for the colonized society and appoint hired or recruited clergy to them. Instead of capturing existing institutions, a parallel religious authority loyal to the empire is created, through which the colonizer attempts to seize spiritual legitimacy from resistance leaders and direct preaching toward the people's subjugation. Unlike Seizure of Religious Institutions (T0100), existing institutions are not subordinated but replaced by an appointee; unlike Religious Assimilation (T0116), the work is carried out within the colonized people's own religion, rather than by converting it to the metropole's confession.

objects.name: Manufacturing a Collaborating Elite
objects.description: Aggressors may cultivate within the colonized society a layer of collaborators, endowing it with power and privileges over their compatriots: offices, salaries, land, decorations and the aggressor's protection. The layer is manufactured, not bought: the aggressor institutes offices and "traditional" authorities where none existed, appoints the executors and binds them by privileges to the aggressor rather than to their own people. The society splits into the aggressor's intermediaries and those governed by them; everyday coercion is carried out by the hands of the colonized themselves, while they answer only to the aggressor. Colonialism scholarship describes the mechanism precisely: the historian Ronald Robinson showed that the colonizer could "manufacture a small modern elite of collaborators and set them in subordinate authority"; the scholar of colonialism Mahmood Mamdani called this construction "decentralized despotism" - "traditional" chiefs appointed by the colonizer receive unlimited power over their own people while answering only to the colonizer.

objects.name: Forced Disarmament
objects.description: Aggressors may systematically confiscate weapons from the colonized population in order to break its capacity for self-defense and revolt. The confiscation is formalized through per-household quotas (for example, one gun from every ten houses) and disguised as a fiscal measure ("in lieu of tribute") or as a "pledge of submission", but the goal is neither revenue nor loot: a disarmed society is left defenseless before the aggressor's troops and the collaborators the aggressor has cultivated, and every new demand can then be imposed without resistance. Disarmament also prepares deeper forms of subjugation - enserfment, conscription, resettlement - which cannot be forced upon an armed society. For societies in which weapons are part of the dignity and status of a free person, their seizure is also a social punishment.

objects.name: Forced Surrender of Fugitives and Rebels
objects.description: Aggressors may impose on subjugated communities the obligation to refuse shelter to members of the resistance and to hand over everyone who has escaped the aggressor's power - rebels, runaway soldiers and bondsmen, prisoners. The obligation is formalized in a decree or a treaty and rests on collective liability: the whole settlement answers for harboring or for failure to inform - with fines, confiscations, devastation. In this way the aggressor destroys the very function of uncontrolled space - mountains, forests, free borderlands - as a refuge beyond its power: political scientist and anthropologist James C. Scott showed that such zones of refuge (he explicitly names the Caucasus among them) are formed by people deliberately fleeing state exactions, and political theorist Neil Roberts described flight from bondage itself as a practice of freedom - the forced surrender of fugitives strikes precisely at it. With the hands of the subjugated themselves, the aggressor turns every settlement that has yielded into a barrier against those still resisting.

objects.name: Forced Public Repentance
objects.description: Aggressors may demand public repentance from the colonized — a ritual of self-abasement involving the renunciation of former loyalties, of the resistance and its leaders, of faith or oaths — as a condition for ending violence, for release, or for the very right to live on one's own land. Repentance is not a mere declaration: it carries consequences. A person's fate hangs on their confession — freedom, prison, or execution. One who has publicly repented is compromised in the eyes of their own people and bound to the aggressor by the public act itself. The aggressor holds up these "voluntary" repentances as proof of its own righteousness and as justification for the repressive character of colonization. Russian colonialism has practiced coerced repentance for centuries: the empire demanded that the highlanders of the Caucasus renounce the "pernicious teaching" of the resistance leader and swear an oath of allegiance to the Russian tsar; Soviet public confessions and denunciations of "enemies of the people" within one's own family, like today's forced video apologies in Chechnya, are a direct continuation of this practice. Since the seizure of Crimea, the practice of forced public repentance — filmed and circulated on social media — has been applied to those who remain loyal to Ukraine or criticize the occupation authorities(Citation: Terror and videoed ‘repentance’ for supporting Ukraine in Russian-occupied Crimea 2023).

external_references.source_name: Terror and videoed ‘repentance’ for supporting Ukraine in Russian-occupied Crimea 2023
external_references.description: Coynash. Terror and videoed ‘repentance’ for supporting Ukraine in Russian-occupied Crimea. 2023.

objects.name: Territorial Marking with Imperial Symbols
objects.description: Aggressors may consolidate the seizure of land with material signs of their own power: crosses and foundation stones at the moment of occupation, monuments to conquerors, memorial plaques and stelae, coats of arms, places of worship raised on the sites of other peoples' sanctuaries. Unlike the renaming of place names, which operates in speech and on the map, a sign occupies physical space and can be removed only by hand. It declares the seizure irreversible and dates the history of the place from the arrival of the metropole: the pedestal of the monument to Bohdan Khmelnytsky in Kyiv (1888) bore the inscription "To Bohdan Khmelnytsky, one and indivisible Russia", while the plaques on the monument to Muravyov-Amursky in Khabarovsk (1891) listed those "who took an active part in the annexation of the Amur region to Russia".

objects.name: Collective Punishment
objects.description: Aggressors may apply collective punishment: for the actions of individuals, reprisals fall on the entire community - villages and districts are subjected to monetary levies, troops are quartered at the residents' expense, families and relatives are exiled, dwellings are demolished, hostages are taken. The prohibition is entrenched in every key codification of the law of war: Article 50 of the Hague Regulations on the Laws and Customs of War on Land (1899, 1907) forbids general penalties imposed on the population for the acts of individuals; Article 33 of the Fourth Geneva Convention (1949) expressly prohibits "collective penalties and likewise all measures of intimidation or of terrorism"; Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions (1977) extends the prohibition to non-international armed conflicts, and the ICRC study of customary international humanitarian law (2005, Rule 103) records it for conflicts of any kind.

objects.name: Sham Trials
objects.description: Aggressors may give reprisal the form of justice by creating and using sham trials: the outcome is predetermined and the defense is absent or ornamental. The forms vary - extraordinary and field courts-martial with a day allotted to a case, closed quasi-judicial bodies passing sentences in absentia and by lists, and show trials staged for the public. Passing sentences without "a regularly constituted court affording all the judicial guarantees" is a war crime (Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions; Article 8(2)(c)(iv) of the Rome Statute, under which the International Criminal Court delivered its first conviction in 2024).

objects.name: Sexualized Violence
objects.description: Aggressors may use sexualized violence as a weapon: rape during punitive operations and sweep operations, sexual torture of detainees, the treatment of captive women as spoils. Such violence targets more than the victim - it terrorizes and humiliates the entire community. Rape, sexual slavery and any other form of sexual violence is a war crime and a crime against humanity (Articles 7(1)(g) and 8(2)(b)(xxii) of the Rome Statute; Article 27 of the Fourth Geneva Convention).

objects.name: Reprisals against Prisoners and Detainees
objects.description: Aggressors may deal reprisals to people who have fallen into their power and take no active part in hostilities - those surrendering, prisoners and detainees, military and civilian alike: issue orders that no quarter be given, kill people as they surrender, execute and torture them in captivity. International law protects this category unconditionally: Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions covers everyone «taking no active part in the hostilities», including those who have laid down their arms and those in detention; the wilful killing of a prisoner of war is a «grave breach» of the Third Convention (Article 130), of a civilian in a party's hands - of the Fourth Convention (Article 147); the Rome Statute treats these acts as war crimes (Articles 8(2)(a)(i), 8(2)(b)(vi), 8(2)(b)(xii) and 8(2)(c)(i)), and attacking persons hors de combat is also prohibited by customary Rule 47 of the study by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

objects.name: Denial of Quarter
objects.description: Aggressors may declare in advance that no quarter will be given: the order to take no prisoners turns every engagement into extermination. The prohibition is explicit: "it is especially forbidden... to declare that no quarter will be given" (Hague Regulations, Article 23(d)); "declaring that no quarter will be given" is a war crime (Rome Statute, Article 8(2)(b)(xii); customary Rule 46 of the ICRC study).

objects.name: Killing of Those Who Surrender
objects.description: Aggressors may kill those who lay down their arms and surrender. This is prohibited by Article 23(c) of the Hague Regulations - "to kill or wound an enemy who, having laid down his arms... has surrendered" - and by the Rome Statute (Article 8(2)(b)(vi)).

objects.name: Killing of Prisoners and Detainees
objects.description: Aggressors may kill prisoners and detainees - people already in their power: without trial, by lists, «while attempting to escape». The wilful killing of a prisoner of war is a «grave breach» of the Third Geneva Convention (Article 130), of a civilian in a party's hands - of the Fourth Convention (Article 147); the killing of any detainee outside combat is prohibited by Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions.

objects.name: Torture and Abuse
objects.description: Aggressors may apply systematic physical and psychological violence against detained members of the local population, prisoners of war, and political activists. The use of brutal interrogations, beatings, and the creation of torturous conditions of detention serves not only the purposes of inquiry but also the total psychological breaking of the society's will, paralyzing its capacity for organized resistance.

objects.name: Desecration of the Dead
objects.description: Aggressors may mock the bodies of the dead - put them on display, carry them around as trophies, refuse families the remains and a place of burial. This is an act aimed at the living: the body is turned into a message to the community, one of intimidation and humiliation. Desecration of bodies is prohibited as an outrage upon personal dignity (Rome Statute, Article 8(2)(b)(xxi); customary Rule 113 of the ICRC study), and the duty to return the remains to the families is fixed by Rule 114.

objects.name: Pillage
objects.description: Aggressors may loot: appropriate residents' property during assaults, sweep operations and searches, divide the "spoils" between soldiers and commanders, carry off livestock, household goods and valuables. Pillage is not limited to combat: on occupied territory it is any appropriation of residents' property - by soldiers or by representatives of the aggressor's administration - for private or institutional benefit without the owner's consent. The Hague Regulations forbid giving up a locality to pillage "even when taken by assault" (Article 28) and "formally forbid" pillage on occupied territory (Article 47); pillaging a town or place is a war crime (Rome Statute, Article 8(2)(b)(xvi)), and both organized seizure of property and acts of individuals for private gain qualify as pillage (ICTY, Celebici case, 1998).

objects.name: Indiscriminate Attacks
objects.description: Aggressors may carry out indiscriminate attacks on places where people live: strike a town or village as a single target, bring down on residential areas blows directed at no specific military objective, use weapons that cannot be aimed or whose effects cannot be limited - from area bombardment to cluster and thermobaric munitions. Additional Protocol I prohibits attacks "which are not directed at a specific military objective" and methods or means "which cannot be directed at a specific military objective" or "the effects of which cannot be limited" (Article 51; customary Rules 11-13 of the ICRC study); the Hague Regulations already forbade "the attack or bombardment, by whatever means, of towns, villages, dwellings, or buildings which are undefended" (Article 25), and the Rome Statute criminalizes attacks on undefended settlements and knowingly disproportionate strikes (Articles 8(2)(b)(v) and 8(2)(b)(iv)).

objects.name: Manufacturing Criminals
objects.description: Aggressors may manufacture "criminals" out of unwanted people: passing laws with offenses elastic enough to charge anyone ("counter-revolutionary activity", "extremism", "discreditation"), inventing conspiracies and underground organizations, forging "evidence", filling cases with people arrested by list, and keeping investigations and trials secret or turning them into public spectacle. Imprisonment becomes a matter of decision rather than fact, and every verdict retroactively "proves" the guilt of the colonized, justifying repression as a fight against "crime".

objects.description: Russian colonialism Matrix

objects.name: Tsardom of Muscovy
objects.description: A historical form of the Russian state (1547–1721).

objects.name: Russian Empire
objects.description: The form of the state from 1721 to 1917, architects of systemic assimilation. The Russian Empire is the successor of the Tsardom of Muscovy, officially proclaimed in 1721. It is characterized by the transition to a regular state, the creation of rigid imperial institutions (the Collegia, the Senate), and the final elimination of treaty-based relations with autonomies. Within the framework, this actor focuses on the unification of governance, the erasure of administrative boundaries, and the complete absorption of local political systems through the bureaucratic apparatus.

objects.name: USSR
objects.description: A totalitarian imperial state, officially proclaimed on December 30, 1922; de facto, a geographic expansion of the regime established by the Bolshevik party in Petrograd in October 1917. It acted as the principal actor of colonial absorption, retention, and exploitation until its collapse in 1991. While formally declaring a union of equal independent republics with the right of free secession, in practice the USSR implemented rigid unification and centralization of governance in Moscow (concentrating absolute power in the Politburo of the Central Committee). This led to the de facto elimination of the political, economic, and cultural sovereignty of the colonized nations. Within the framework, this actor is characterized by an unprecedented scale of social engineering: total control over society, the dissemination of information, the economy, and education; the use of institutional terror; the physical annihilation of the peasantry through artificial famine; mass ethnic cleansing by deporting peoples to other regions of the empire; as well as a policy of systematic Russification and the destruction/incorporation/Russification of national elites.

objects.name: Russian Federation
objects.description: A state formation since 1991. It acts as an actor employing both inherited imperial instruments of hard power (military intervention, puppet governments, mass killings) and modern methods of control (economic and transport blockades, proxy wars through security services, cyberattacks, networked propaganda, and indoctrination).

objects.name: Russian Republic
objects.description: A state formation on the territory of the former Russian Empire, proclaimed after the February Revolution. It was governed by the Provisional Government. It existed from March to November 1917, after which it was overthrown as a result of the Bolshevik coup.

objects.name: Soviet Russia (RSFSR)
objects.description: A state formed as a result of the Bolshevik coup in November 1917 (official name from July 1918: the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic). It acted as the principal actor of military expansion, hybrid war, and the colonial absorption of the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR) in 1917–1922. In December 1922 it became a co-founder and the core part of the USSR.

objects.name: White Movement (AFSR)
objects.description: A military-political movement (the Armed Forces of South Russia) that advocated the restoration of a "one and indivisible" Russia. In 1918–1920 it conducted combat operations on the territory of Ukraine against both the Bolsheviks and the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR), denying Ukraine's right to independence.

objects.name: Pereiaslav Council (1654)
objects.description: The oath of Bohdan Khmelnytsky and the starshyna to the tsar. Establishment of control over the Hetmanate through a legal trap: the treaty was asymmetric by design – in response to the demand for a mutual oath, envoy "V. Buturlin, citing the autocratic character of the Russian monarch's power, refused to do so"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011). The very language of "reunification" is a later imperial overlay: Tsar Aleksei's charter to the Zaporozhian Host (27 March 1654) speaks only of subjects who "have come under our sovereign's high hand"(Citation: Жалованная грамота царя Алексея Михайловича Войску Запорожскому 1654).

objects.description: Open military aggression by the Tsardom of Muscovy in response to the hetman's attempt to break vassalage. objects.name: Truce of Andrusovo (1667)
objects.description: An agreement on the partition of the Hetmanate along the Dnipro between the Tsardom of Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth without Ukrainian participation: "The Russian state received significant territorial acquisitions… However, Right-Bank Ukraine, Polotsk, Vitebsk, and other Belarusian cities with Russian garrisons remained with the Commonwealth"(Citation: Андрусовское перемирие 1667 2005). The legal entrenchment of Ukraine's split and the transformation of Zaporizhzhia into a buffer zone: "under the treaty of 1667 it was under the joint rule of Moscow and Warsaw"(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011). Hrushevsky records the reaction to the partition: "there was great resentment against the Muscovite government for agreeing to cede Right-Bank Ukraine to Poland in the armistice of 1667: it divided Ukraine with Poland and did not keep what it had promised when taking Ukraine under the tsar's hand"(Citation: Ілюстрована історія України 1921).

История «предательства» 2011).

objects.name: Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690)
objects.description: The annexation of the independent Ukrainian church through diplomatic pressure and corruption. Patriarch Dositheus of Jerusalem directly accused the Muscovite envoys of simony: "What fault is it to tear away another's eparchy? Is it not a shame before people, is it not a sin before God! You send money and lead people out of their minds, you take charters contrary to the church and to God"(Citation: Архив Юго-Западной России. Часть 1. Том V 1872). The subordination of the church was justified by geopolitics: "Golitsyn's main project… was the reform of the Ukrainian Orthodox church, or rather – the subordination of the Kyiv metropolitanate to the Moscow patriarch"(Citation: Мазепа 2007).

objects.name: "Eternal Peace" with Poland (1686)
objects.description: The legal legitimation of the partition of territories between the Tsardom of Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth behind the Hetmanate's back, definitively turning Ukraine into a rightless object of bargaining. The deal was sealed financially – under the text of the 1686 treaty Moscow undertook "for eternal peace to count out a genuine sum of money, that is, one hundred forty-six thousand Muscovite rubles, and hand it over to the Commonwealth"(Citation: Сборник грамот и договоров о присоединении царств и областей 1922). "Russian historians usually assess the Eternal Peace as Golitsyn's great diplomatic success, Polish ones – as their major defeat, and contemporary Ukrainian ones – as a national tragedy of Ukraine"(Citation: Мазепа 2007).

objects.name: Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708)
objects.description: In response to the autonomy's attempt to break vassalage, the regular Muscovite army destroyed the hetman's capital, Baturyn. Peter ordered: "and Baturyn, as a sign to the traitors (since they resisted), burn down entirely as an example to others"(Citation: Мазепа 2007). The reprisal was accompanied by terror against the civilian population: "Funck slaughtered more than a thousand people in the small town of Terey (Tereyska sloboda) and burned the town down"(Citation: Сочинения в 12 томах. Том 10 1959), and in total "about 15 thousand Ukrainians died in the Baturyn tragedy, including all the women and children"(Citation: Мазепа 2007). The massacre ran in parallel with propaganda: "Tsarist letters were circulated among the people claiming that Mazepa had gone over to the Swedes in order to hand Ukraine to Poland, to introduce the Union in Ukraine and eradicate the pious faith; that he was an apostate, a secret Catholic"(Citation: Ілюстрована історія України 1921).

objects.name: The Lebedyn Executions (1708–1709)
objects.description: A punitive campaign against Mazepa's supporters after the hetman went over to the Swedes. In January 1709 the headquarters of the tsar and Menshikov were at Lebedyn and Sumy, from where the investigation of the Cossack officers was conducted(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011). The model of intimidation was the destruction of the hetman capital: on 2 November 1708 Baturyn was taken by Menshikov's troops, "the town was razed to the ground and its inhabitants annihilated," and when in July 1709 the tsar permitted it to be resettled, he obliged the inhabitants to pay a special tax to the treasury "for treason"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003). The punishment fell on everyone: "in the bloody massacre and fire a multitude of the town's defenders and inhabitants perished"(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011).

objects.name: Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1709)
objects.description: A military operation of Muscovite troops to completely destroy the Zaporozhian (Chortomlyk) Sich as an autonomous military center in revenge for its support of Charles XII: "Having lost the proxy battle for Zaporizhzhia, Peter decided to follow the path of Baturyn — to destroy the Sich"(Citation: Мазепа 2007). Contemporaries recorded the empire's goal directly – Orlyk wrote that Moscow intended "to eradicate the Zaporozhian Host of the Lower Dnipro and to efface its very name forever"(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011).

objects.name: The Battle of Poltava and the Final Defeat of the Hetmanate (1709)
objects.description: The decisive battle of the Great Northern War, in the course of which the military backbone of Ukrainian autonomy was finally eliminated. The defeat of the Swedish-Cossack alliance allowed Moscow to move from suppressing uprisings to the systematic dismantling of the Hetmanate's political agency(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011).

The articles "fully preserved the previously established control of the tsarist regime over local financing, the functioning of the administrative apparatus, the Cossack army, and foreign policy"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 9 2012).

objects.name: The Case of Pavlo Polubotok (1723)
objects.description: Peter I's establishment of the First Little Russian Collegium to seize governance from the hetman's administration: the collegium was created "as the highest appellate instance and the administrative-controlling organ of the Russian state structure in Ukraine"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 6 2009). It was accompanied by the arrest of acting hetman Polubotok and the officers for defending the autonomy: "the officers submitted to Emperor Peter I yet another petition to close the Little Russian Collegium. After this, interrogations of Polubotok began in the Secret Chancellery, and on November 10, 1723 he was arrested and imprisoned in the Peter and Paul Fortress"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011), where the hetman died. The arrest order itself was never published as a separate act - the case was run by the Secret Chancellery; the circumstances were retrospectively set out in Empress Catherine I's manifesto of 8 February 1725: "it was ordered that the General Starshyna - Polubotok, Chernysh and Savych - be in St. Petersburg to answer for it"(Citation: Полное собрание законов Российской империи. Собрание первое. Том VII (1723-1727) 1830).

objects.name: Forced Labor on Imperial Construction: The Ladoga Canal (1704–1725)
objects.description: The physical and economic exhaustion of the region through the transformation of the Cossack host into unpaid labor for imperial construction projects. The chief of these was the Ladoga Canal: Peter I handed the direction of the works to Münnich, while the digging itself "was carried out chiefly by the hands of Ukrainian Cossacks," and "on the construction works, tens of thousands of people perished from back-breaking labor, hunger and the harsh climate"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 6 2009). In 1721 the acting hetman P. Polubotok "headed a 10,000-strong Cossack corps dispatched by order of Tsar Peter I to the construction of the Ladoga Canal"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011). For the defiant there were also the Neva construction sites - as hard labor: captured Zaporozhians were "exiled to Sankt-Piterburkh to hard labor forever"(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011).

objects.name: Creation of the Little Russian Prikaz (1663)
objects.description: Institutional substitution: Ukrainian affairs were handed over to a special agency in Moscow. The Little Russian Prikaz was founded "as one of the departments of the Ambassadorial Prikaz to administer Ukrainian affairs," and through it the tsarist government "exercised control over the political-administrative activity of the hetman's administration and the tsarist voivodes in Ukraine"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 6 2009) – the Hetmanate fell under the permanent departmental oversight of the metropole.

objects.name: The Moscow Articles of Ivan Briukhovetsky (1665)
objects.description: The treaty that became the point of no return in the political, economic, and military absorption of the autonomy: "Under the Moscow Articles, direct control over the military-administrative and financial-economic life of Ukraine (except for the Cossack estate) passed into the hands of the tsarist voivodes"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 7 2010). Garrisons headed by voivodes were introduced into new cities as far as Kodak, taxes went directly to the tsar's treasury, and the Kyiv metropolitanate was to be subordinated to the Moscow patriarch(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 7 2010).

objects.name: The Konotop Articles of Ivan Samoilovych (1672)
objects.description: A further curtailment of the Hetmanate's political agency and interference in the autonomy's internal affairs: "Overall, the Konotop Articles limited the hetman's power in favor of the officer oligarchy, and also narrowed the autonomy of the Hetmanate"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008). The weakening of the hetman's power laid the ground for the growing influence of the Muscovite government over the autonomy's elites.

objects.name: Liquidation of the Cossacks in Right-Bank Ukraine (1699)
objects.description: The destruction of the Cossack regimental order on the Right Bank by a decision of the Polish Sejm of 1699, on lands that Moscow and Warsaw had divided along the Dnipro by the "Eternal Peace" of 1686. Colonel Palii "did not accept the decisions of the general Sejm of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth of 1699 banning the Cossacks on the Right Bank" and "contrary to the terms of the 'Eternal Peace' of 1686 pursued a policy of uniting the Right Bank and the Left Bank"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011).

objects.name: Pylyp Orlyk's Campaign in Right-Bank Ukraine (1711)
objects.description: A military-diplomatic attempt to restore Ukraine's independence by the forces of the emigration with the support of allies. The campaign failed because of a stab in the back: "the Tatars, disobeying Orlyk, scattered in raiding parties and began taking yasyr captives across Ukrainian villages"(Citation: Мазепинці 1885).

objects.name: The Decisive Points (1728)
objects.description: A unilateral imperial act imposed on hetman Danylo Apostol instead of the traditional bilateral treaty. While formally softening the regime of the Little Russian Collegium, the document entrenched harsh imperial restrictions on key points: "Article 19 forbids the hetman relations with other countries"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 9 2012), customs revenues went to the tsar's treasury, and personnel appointments were placed under the metropole's control.

objects.name: The Governing Council of the Hetman Government and the Lubny Treaty (1734–1750)
objects.description: A long period of direct rule over the Left Bank without the election of a hetman. "The GOVERNANCE OF THE HETMAN'S GOVERNMENT was an organ of power created by the government of Russian empress Anna in 1734 after the death of hetman D. Apostol to govern Left-Bank Ukraine (the Hetmanate) and to prevent new hetman elections"; "in essence its head was the tsar's resident"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011). At the same time the empire brought Zaporizhzhia back under control: "Anna amnestied the Zaporozhians and allowed them to return to the old Sich grounds (1734) and found the New Sich"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003) – on the eve of war with Turkey the Cossacks were being brought back as a military resource of the crown.

objects.name: Liquidation of the Institution of the Hetmancy and the Second Little Russian Collegium (1764)
objects.description: The final abolition of political autonomy. Catherine II forced hetman Rozumovsky to renounce his office and by the decree of November 10, 1764 established an occupation administration: "we command our Senate, for the proper governance of Little Russia, to establish there a Little Russian Collegium, presided over by our general, Count Rumyantsev"(Citation: Указ об учреждении Малороссийской коллегии 1764). The program had been set in advance in a secret instruction: "so that they become Russified and cease looking to the forest like wolves"(Citation: Наставление Екатерины II князю Вяземскому 1764).

objects.name: Abolition of the Cossack Order in Sloboda Ukraine (1765)
objects.description: An imperial reform to liquidate the military-social structure of Sloboda Ukraine: "The conclusions of this investigation, with the participation of a Senate commission, led to the verdict of the Governing Senate on the liquidation of the autonomous order on December 16, 1764, and a series of experimental innovations approved by Catherine II's manifesto of July 28, 1765. On the basis of the Sloboda regiments the Sloboda-Ukrainian Governorate was formed, out of the military forces – 5 hussar regiments of the same names (see Hussars), and the bulk of the Cossack population was transferred to the category of military settlers"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 9 2012).

objects.name: Russo-Turkish War and the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1768–1774)
objects.description: The use of Ukrainian resources and Cossack regiments for victory over the Ottomans on the Danube. The diplomatic severing of Crimea from the Ottoman Empire through the recognition of a fictitious "independence": under Article III of the treaty, "All the Tatar peoples: the Crimean, Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk, and Yedichkul, without exception, are to be recognized by both empires as free and entirely independent of any outside power"(Citation: Кючук-Кайнарджийский мирный договор 1774) – this "independence" became the prologue to the annexation of the peninsula nine years later.

objects.name: Military Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1775)
objects.description: The military encirclement and destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich immediately after a joint war. Catherine II's manifesto of 3 August 1775 (PSZRI, coll. 1, vol. XX, no. 14,354) declared: "the Zaporozhian Sich has been utterly destroyed, with the extirpation for the future of the very name of the Zaporozhian Cossacks"(Citation: Манифест об уничтожении Запорожской Сечи 1775)(Citation: Полное собрание законов Российской империи. Собрание первое. Том XX (1775-1780) 1830). The last kish otaman, Kalnyshevsky, "was arrested and sent to the prison of the Solovetsky monastery"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 4 2007), where he spent more than 25 years. Hrushevsky describes the mechanics of the treachery: the government "went about the affair slowly, in secret, to catch the Zaporozhians entirely unprepared," and general Tekeli "entered the Zaporozhian lands as a good friend" - then suddenly laid siege to the Sich. The Zaporozhians were even faulted for their own husbandry: they "were establishing their own tillage and thereby severing their dependence on the Russian state"(Citation: Ілюстрована історія України 1921).

objects.name: Military Annexation of the Crimean Khanate (1783)
objects.description: The seizure of the Crimean Khanate and its forcible incorporation into the Russian Empire: "WE have resolved to take under OUR dominion the Crimean peninsula, the island of Taman, and the entire Kuban side"(Citation: Манифест о принятии Крыма под Российскую державу 1783). With regard to Ukraine, the annexation was secured through the forced mobilization of Cossacks as a military resource, the colonization of the adjacent southern steppes to create a loyal rear, and the erasure of Cossack toponyms: the lands of the destroyed Sich were assigned by Catherine II's manifesto of 3 August 1775 "as convenient to the Novorossiysk Governorate"(Citation: Манифест об уничтожении Запорожской Сечи 1775). For Crimea this meant the liquidation of the state and its ruling dynasty: "in the spring of 1782 Khan Shahin Girey was forced to flee under Russian protection"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008), the manifesto on the taking of Crimea was signed by Catherine II on April 8, 1783 (PSZRI, coll. 1, vol. XXI, no. 15,108)(Citation: Полное собрание законов Российской империи. Собрание первое. Том XXI (1781-1783) 1830), and the khan was exiled to Kaluga; the indigenous population was being squeezed out in waves of emigration - "if before 1787 only 8 thousand had emigrated, by 1792 it was already tens of thousands"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008).

objects.name: Establishment of the "Pale of Settlement" (1791)
objects.description: The introduction of discriminatory legislation that territorially restricted the rights of the Jewish population: decree No. 17,006 of December 23, 1791 confirmed the ban on Jews enrolling in the merchantry in the internal Russian cities and ports, extending the rights of citizenship and burgher status only to the Ekaterinoslav Viceroyalty and the Tauride region(Citation: Указ о правах гражданства евреев 1791). From the totality of such acts emerged the Pale of Settlement, running predominantly through colonized Ukrainian territories.

objects.name: Second and Third Partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (1793–1795)
objects.description: The Russian Empire's collusion with the Hohenzollern and Habsburg monarchies to dismember a neighboring state. Under the second partition, "Russia received the central part of Belarus, the Kyiv, Bratslav, and Podillia voivodeships, and the eastern half of the Volhynian voivodeship – in total 250 thousand km2 and over 3 million inhabitants," and after the third, "the Polish state ceased to exist"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011).

objects.description: The use of Ukrainian resources in yet another geopolitical war of the empire, which ended with the severing of Bessarabia from the Ottoman Empire: "After the incorporation of Bessarabia into Russia on May 16, 1812 (see the Treaty of Bucharest of 1812), Ukrainian Cossacks of the volunteer regiments, of the Ust-Danube Budjak Cossack Host, and of the Danube Cossack Host actively settled the Budjak"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003).

objects.name: War with Napoleon: Forced Mobilization and Deception (1812)
objects.description: The authorities' false promise to return the lost Cossack liberties to the indigenous population in exchange for blood. The empire squeezed the maximum out of the land: "on both of its banks, Ukraine was used for the recruitment, equipping, and movement of troops… including a 75-thousand-strong militia from the Kyiv, Podillia, Chernihiv, and Poltava governorates"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003), and after the war the formations were disbanded and the promises forgotten(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 7 2010); when the Buh Cossacks refused to be turned into military settlers in 1817, their uprising was crushed by four regiments with artillery(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003).

objects.name: Introduction of Military Settlements and Liquidation of the Danubian Sich (1817–1828)
objects.description: A campaign to turn the free population into rightless military settlers. "The trigger was the order abolishing the Buh Cossack Host and turning the Cossacks into military settlers"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003) – the Buh Cossacks' uprising of 1817 was brutally suppressed. There were two acts, on opposite sides of the uprising: the nominal decree of April 17, 1817 transferred the Buh Host's district "into direct military administration" (PSZRI, vol. XXXIV, no. 26,802) - this was the trigger; the decree of October 8, 1817 (no. 27,081), issued after the suppression, formalized the liquidation: "the name of the Buh Cossack Host is abolished"(Citation: Полное собрание законов Российской империи. Собрание первое. Том XXXIV (1817) 1830). Later, kish otaman Hladky with part of the Danubian Cossacks "on May 30 (18), 1828 crossed the Kiliya mouth of the Danube, entered the port of Izmail, and joined the Russian army"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 3 2005) – this was the end of the last free host: the Danubian Sich "existed from the last quarter of the 18th century until 1828"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 3 2005).

objects.name: Destruction of the Archives of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra (1718)
objects.description: A covert operation (sabotage) by Muscovite emissaries disguised as monks, aimed at the physical destruction of historical archives. According to testimonies preserved by the Kyiv scholar Lebedyntsev, "the Lavra was set on fire by emissaries from Moscow dressed as monks. The enormous archive and library burned down; the charters and grants… of princes, magnates, and hetmans perished"; historian Hyrych sums up: "The fire destroyed the written memory of the Lavra's independent Ukrainian political and spiritual life"(Citation: Що замовчують екскурсоводи у Києво-Печерській лаврі 2018).

objects.name: Ban on Ukrainian Book Printing (1720)
objects.description: A campaign to introduce censorship and institutional linguistic assimilation. Peter I's decree of October 5, 1720 banned the printing of books in the indigenous people's language at the key printing houses: "In the Kyiv-Pechersk and Chernihiv printing houses no new books whatsoever are to be printed except previous church editions, and even those old church books are to be corrected before printing for complete conformity with the Great Russian church books, so that there be no discord or distinct dialect in them"(Citation: Указ Петра I о книгопечатании 1720).

objects.name: The Ems Ukaz and Total Censorship (1876–1887)
objects.description:
The complete displacement of the language from the cultural and literary sphere. The Ems ukase prescribed: "Not to permit the import into the empire… of any books whatsoever published abroad in the Little Russian dialect," "To forbid in the empire the printing, in the same dialect, of any original works or translations whatsoever," and "To forbid likewise any stage performances, texts to musical scores, and public readings in the same dialect"(Citation: Эмский указ 1876). The permitted dictionaries were allowed only "on condition of their being printed in conformity with all-Russian orthography"(Citation: Навічно кували кайдани 1995).

Five years later the rules were revised by a Special Conference - it included Solsky, Ostrovsky, the chief procurator of the Synod Pobedonostsev, and Viazemsky, - and the minister of internal affairs Ignatiev reported the result to the emperor on 3 October 1881; assent followed on 8 October(Citation: Українська ідентичність і мовне питання в Російській імперії 2013). There were no plans to publish the revision, and Ignatiev explained why: "the rules on the use of the Little Russian dialect established in 1876 were not promulgated, and therefore it is not intended to make the projected clarifications known to the general public"(Citation: Українська ідентичність і мовне питання в Російській імперії 2013). The circular went out to governor-general Drenteln on 16 October stamped "Confidential"(Citation: Українська ідентичність і мовне питання в Російській імперії 2013) - that is, people were judged by rules they were never shown.

objects.name: Ban on the Language in Books and Public Speeches (1892–1905)
objects.description: A state campaign to drive the language out of public space and literature: in 1892 the Main Administration for Press Affairs directed the censorship committee to suppress translations into Ukrainian, "reducing the number of such talentless works for purely state purposes"(Citation: Об отмене стеснений малорусского печатного слова 1905); at the archaeological congress in Kyiv in 1899, scholars from Austrian-ruled Ukraine were forbidden to read papers in Ukrainian - in protest they withdrew from participation(Citation: Українська мова в першій половині двадцятого століття (1900-1941). Стан і статус 1987); at the unveiling of the Kotliarevsky monument in Poltava on 30-31 August 1903, only guests from Galicia were allowed to speak Ukrainian, while the mayor forbade the locals to do so, citing an order of the ministry of internal affairs(Citation: Українська мова в першій половині двадцятого століття (1900-1941). Стан і статус 1987). Even children's literature fell under the ban: the 1895 circular prohibited Ukrainian books "for children's reading"(Citation: Навічно кували кайдани 1995).

objects.name: Destruction of Ukrainian Societies and Segregation (1906–1910)
objects.description: A campaign to suppress the legal civic activity of the indigenous people: in the Poltava and Kharkiv regions the "Prosvita" societies were banned from their very founding, and in 1908–1910, under Stolypin, virtually all "Prosvitas" were closed, except the branches of the Katerynoslav governorate(Citation: Українська мова в першій половині двадцятого століття (1900-1941). Стан і статус 1987). Justifying the crackdown, Stolypin declared in an address to the Senate that the revival of Ukrainian cultural life was undesirable, for "the three principal branches of Eastern Slavdom, both by origin and by language, cannot but constitute one whole"(Citation: Українська мова в першій половині двадцятого століття (1900-1941). Стан і статус 1987). Stolypin's circular of 1910 classed Ukrainians among the "aliens" and prescribed "to refuse without fail the registration" of their societies(Citation: Столыпинский циркуляр 1910).

objects.name: Ban on Culture and the Press Before World War I (1913–1914)
objects.description: The Russian Empire continued destroying the indigenous people's culture on the eve of the war: the curator of the Kyiv school district, Derevytsky, in 1913 "issued an instruction in which he declared students' attendance of Ukrainian theatrical performances as inadmissible as spending time in billiard halls or beer houses, and in 1914 categorically forbade all educational institutions of the Kyiv district to mark the 100th jubilee of Taras Shevchenko"(Citation: Наша пісня гарна й нова? 2013); with the outbreak of the war, Nicholas II by a personal decree of 20 July 1914 introduced military censorship with the command's right "to suspend periodical publications"(Citation: Указ об утверждении временного Положения о военной цензуре 1914) - and that very day the military authorities of the Kyiv military district closed the only Ukrainian daily newspaper, "Rada"(Citation: Українська мова в першій половині двадцятого століття (1900-1941). Стан і статус 1987).

objects.name: Stalinist Terror and the End of Ukrainization (1922–1939)
objects.description: The suppression of the national revival in the USSR: the resolution of the Central Committee of the VKP(b) and the Council of People's Commissars of 14 December 1932, signed by Stalin and Molotov, declared that "Ukrainization was carried out mechanically" and ordered "to immediately transfer in the North Caucasus the record-keeping of the soviet and cooperative bodies of the 'Ukrainized' districts, as well as all published newspapers and journals, from the Ukrainian language to Russian"(Citation: О хлебозаготовках на Украине, Северном Кавказе и в Западной области 1932); the annihilation of most Ukrainian writers of the 1920s-1930s went down in history as the "Executed Renaissance"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 9 2012); the resolution of the USSR Council of People's Commissars and the Central Committee of the VKP(b) of 13 March 1938 No. 324 ordered "to introduce the teaching of the Russian language as a subject of study in the schools of the national republics and regions from September 1, 1938"(Citation: Об обязательном изучении русского языка в школах национальных республик и областей 1938).

objects.name: Creation of a Single "Soviet People" (1958–1970)
objects.description: The USSR's official campaign to erase national distinctions: The start was given by the USSR Law "On Strengthening the Connection of School with Life and on the Further Development of the System of Public Education in the USSR" of December 24, 1958: it contained no direct norm on language, leaving the matter to the republics(Citation: Закон «Об укреплении связи школы с жизнью и о дальнейшем развитии системы народного образования в СССР» 1958); the republican Law of the Ukrainian SSR of April 17, 1959, by its Article 9, made the choice of the language of instruction a matter for parents(Citation: Україна: хроніка ХХ століття. 1946-1960 2005). The Third Program of the CPSU, adopted by the 22nd Congress in October 1961, proclaimed "a new stage in the development of national relations in the USSR, characterized by the further drawing together of nations and the achievement of their complete unity" - up to and including "the effacement of national distinctions, especially of language distinctions"(Citation: Программа Коммунистической партии Советского Союза 1961).

objects.name: Financial Russification of Schools (1978–1983)
objects.description: The Soviet Union introduced a system of direct material incentives for assimilation: pursuant to the resolution of the USSR Council of Ministers of 13 October 1978 No. 835 "On measures for the further improvement of the study and teaching of the Russian language in the union republics," the Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR, by its resolution of 2 November 1978 No. 518, introduced the study of Russian from the first grades of Ukrainian schools starting with the 1980/81 school year(Citation: Про заходи по дальшому удосконаленню вивчення і викладання російської мови в Українській РСР 1978); the all-Union conference "The Russian Language — the Language of Friendship and Cooperation of the Peoples of the USSR" (Tashkent, 22–24 May 1979) spelled out Russification measures down to kindergartens(Citation: Навічно кували кайдани 1995); the resolution of the CPSU Central Committee and the USSR Council of Ministers of 26 May 1983 No. 473 "On additional measures for improving the study of the Russian language in general-education schools and other educational institutions of the union republics" and the resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Ukraine and the Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR of 10 June 1983 raised the salary rates of Russian-language teachers by 15 percent from 1984(Citation: Навічно кували кайдани 1995)(Citation: Школа і мова. Про доплати вчителям мови/язика нині і в минулому 2018).

objects.name: Suppression of the November Uprising (1830–1831)
objects.description: The Russian Empire's regular army suppresses a national liberation uprising: the insurgent detachments in Volhynia, the Zhytomyr region, Podillia, and the Kyiv region "were routed by the tsarist troops in April–May 1831," after which "the tsarist government resorted to brutal repressions against the participants of the uprising"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011). The era of tightening the screws on the Right Bank begins.

objects.name: Crushing of the Cyril and Methodius Society (1847)
objects.description: The secret police's blow against the intellectual elite of the indigenous people: "In March 1847 the society was crushed by the gendarmes. The police managed to identify 12 members of the clandestine organization… The tsarist authorities judged the society's program documents a serious threat to the foundations of autocracy"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 4 2007). The sentences for all the accused were proposed by the chief of gendarmes Orlov in his report to the emperor of May 26, 1847, on which Nicholas I inscribed "Execute"(Citation: Кирило-Мефодіївське товариство: У 3 т. 1990). It was accompanied by trials, exiles, and Shevchenko's dispatch into the army "with the institution over the poet of 'the strictest surveillance with a prohibition on writing and drawing'"(Citation: Труды и дни Кобзаря 1996).

objects.name: The Bohdan Khmelnytsky Monument (1888)
objects.description: In 1888 the Russian Empire put up in central Kyiv a monument to Bohdan Khmelnytsky - a sign of the city's belonging to the empire and of "unity" with Moscow. The pedestal bore programmatic inscriptions: "We will to be under the tsar of the east, the Orthodox one" and "To Bohdan Khmelnytsky – one and indivisible Russia"(Citation: Пам'ятник Богдану Хмельницькому в Києві 2026). The monument was unveiled on 11 July 1888 on Sophia Square; the committee for its construction was headed by Mikhail Yuzefovich - an official of the Kyiv educational district and author of the memorandum that formed the basis of the Ems ukase of 1876(Citation: Пам'ятник Богдану Хмельницькому в Києві 2026)(Citation: 1876 - підписано Емський указ 2026).

objects.name: The "Historical Path" (1909–1911)
objects.description: The Kyiv section of the Imperial Russian Military-Historical Society was filling central Kyiv with monuments to "figures of Russian history" and pushed the Shevchenko monument, which the city had already decided to put up, off its allotted site. The queue of eight imperial monuments - from princess Olha to Nestor the chronicler - was submitted in a memorandum of 7 April 1910 by colonel Steletsky, the section's secretary(Citation: «Исторический путь» у Києві 1926). The "historical path" program grew out of a letter from Zilov, the trustee of the educational district, to governor-general Trepov: Shevchenko should not be placed opposite a "Russian governmental institution," and "it would be necessary to put up a monument to one of the figures of Russian history"(Citation: «Исторический путь» у Києві 1926). The only monument of the queue actually put up was princess Olha (4 September 1911) - on the site the city had allotted in 1909 for the Shevchenko monument and which the duma gave to the society in 1911, overturning its own decision(Citation: «Исторический путь» у Києві 1926).

objects.name: The Alexander II Monument in Kyiv (1911)
objects.description: In 1911 the Russian Empire put up in central Kyiv the largest monument to Alexander II in the entire empire. The monument was unveiled on 30 August 1911 on Tsarskaya Square; the money was raised by an all-Russian subscription, 200 thousand rubles; the central pedestal bore the coat of arms of the empire, the double-headed eagle, and the inscription "To the Tsar-Liberator, the grateful Southwestern Krai. The year 1911"(Citation: Скільки пам'ятнику стояти? 2004)(Citation: Памятник царю-освободителю императору Александру II 2026).

objects.name: Industrial Colonization and Resource Exploitation of the South (1890)
objects.description: At the end of the 19th century, the Russian Empire turns the Ukrainian lands into a raw-materials colony, exploiting the resources of the Donbas and deliberately importing labor: "42 percent of the 425,413 workers counted in the census were born outside Ukraine," and "in 1892, 80 percent of the workforce at the mines and plants of Yuzivka… had arrived from the Moscow region"(Citation: Соціальні зміни і національна свідомість в Україні ХХ століття 1997).

objects.name: All-Russian Census and the Erasure of Identity (1897)
objects.description: The empire conducted the general census of 1897, embedded in the doctrine of the "triune Russian people". The linguist Sergei Bulich, in his article for the Brockhaus and Efron Encyclopedic Dictionary, classified Ukrainian speech thus: "the Little Russian dialect of the Russian language"(Citation: Малорусское наречие 1896). Historians of the Institute of History of Ukraine of the National Academy of Sciences note: "The census of 1897 recorded not nationality but the respondents' native tongue, and since many Ukrainians named Russian as such, there were in fact more ethnic Ukrainians than indicated in the census"(Citation: Національне питання в Україні ХХ – початку ХХІ ст. 2012). The census also recorded the reach of the Ukrainian language. According to its consolidated volume, the "Little Russian dialect" - the imperial name for the Ukrainian language - was named as their native tongue by 22,380,551 people out of 125,640,021 counted in the empire, that is 17.8%: the empire's second language by number of speakers after Great Russian (Russian)(Citation: Общий свод по Империи результатов разработки данных Первой всеобщей переписи населения, произведенной 28 января 1897 года. Т. 2 1905). Nearly one in four speakers lived outside the nine Ukrainian governorates, and in the Kuban region (now mostly Krasnodar krai of Russia) Ukrainian was the most widespread native language(Citation: Общий свод по Империи результатов разработки данных Первой всеобщей переписи населения, произведенной 28 января 1897 года. Т. 2 1905).

objects.name: Failure of the Political Seizure of the UNR in Kyiv (November – December 1917)
objects.description: The first attempt by Soviet Russia (the Russian Soviet Republic) to liquidate Ukraine's independence by hijacking power at the All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets. The Bolshevik government (the Sovnarkom) planned to plant its delegates, artificially create a majority, and legally vote to transfer power to the Soviets under its control. objects.name: Soviet-Ukrainian War: First Invasion and the Puppet Government (December 1917 - April 1918)
objects.description: In December 1917, Soviet Russia began its first armed invasion of Ukraine, disguising it as an internal war. Defeated in Kyiv, supporters of the Bolsheviks moved to Kharkiv, held an alternative congress there, and created a puppet government - the People's Secretariat: "the first Soviet government of Ukraine," created "as an alternative to the Ukrainian Central Rada and the General Secretariat of the Ukrainian Central Rada"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 7 2010). Thus began the Soviet-Ukrainian War (1917-1921): Soviet Russia passed off the invasion by its own troops as an internal civil war(Citation: Україна й українці в постімперську добу (1917—1939) 2021)(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003). In February 1918, RSFSR troops under the command of Muravyov captured Kyiv and carried out a massacre there; historians call Muravyov "the initiator of mass executions in the city"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 7 2010). The invasion was stopped by the Brest-Litovsk peace treaty (9 February 1918) - the first international act to recognize the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR) as a subject of international law. At the request of the UNR government, German and Austro-Hungarian troops entered Ukraine, and by the end of April 1918 they had driven the RSFSR troops from all Ukrainian land(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003). After Germany's capitulation in November 1918 these troops left - and Soviet Russia invaded again (campaign C0074).

objects.name: The Battle of Kruty and the Killing of Prisoners (January 1918)
objects.description: In late December 1917, as the troops of Bolshevik Russia were advancing on Kyiv, a detachment of yunkers - cadets of the 1st Kyiv Youth Military School named after Bohdan Khmelnytsky (four companies of 150 cadets each, 20 officers, 18 machine guns) - under the command of Sotnyk Averkii Honcharenko took up the defense of Bakhmach station, a railway junction on the border of the UNR and the RSFSR(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008). On January 27, 1918, reinforcements arrived from Kyiv - the first company of the student volunteer battalion under the command of Sotnyk Omelchenko, 115-130 volunteers: students of the Ukrainian National University and Kyiv University and senior-grade pupils of Ukrainian gymnasiums - teenagers, many of them 17 years old(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008)(Citation: Слідча справа М.А.Муравйова: Документована історія 2001). The Ukrainian forces took up defense near Kruty station (now the village of Pamiatne in Chernihiv oblast)(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008). On the morning of January 29 a six-thousand-strong detachment of Petrograd and Moscow Red Guards led by Yegorov attacked the positions; the fighting lasted until evening, the defenders repelled several attacks and, on the order of Sotnyk Averkii Honcharenko, withdrew to their echelon - the detachment's train waiting two kilometers away; their losses came to as many as 300 killed, wounded, and captured(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008). A platoon of the student company lost its bearings at dusk and came out at the station already held by the Red Guards; 27 prisoners were shot - among them, according to testimony in the investigation file of commander-in-chief Muravyov, "there were many gymnasium pupils of about 17"; Yegorov, commander of the First Revolutionary Army, authorized the shooting(Citation: Слідча справа М.А.Муравйова: Документована історія 2001). The teenage cadets managed to delay the offensive: explaining the heavy losses at Kruty and the delay in the advance on Kyiv, Muravyov claimed in his report that the Ukrainian forces had been commanded by "S. Petliura himself" - as the compilers of the collection of the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory note(Citation: Бій під Крутами в національній пам'яті: Збірник документів і матеріалів 2013). In February Muravyov's troops approached Kyiv from the Darnytsia side, shelled the city with heavy artillery for five days, and captured it on February 8, 1918(Citation: Ленінська система влади і власності в окупованій Україні. 1917—1923 2024). After the UNR concluded the Peace of Brest-Litovsk with the Central Powers, German and Austro-Hungarian troops entered Ukraine, with Ukrainian units in the vanguard; the Bolsheviks abandoned Kyiv, and in early March the Council of People's Ministers returned there, followed a few days later by the Ukrainian Central Rada(Citation: Нариси історії Української революції 1917–1921 років: Кн. 1 2011). On March 19, 1918, by decision of the Ukrainian Central Rada, the bodies of those killed at Kruty were brought to Kyiv and ceremonially buried at the Askold's Grave cemetery(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 5 2008).

objects.name: Artificial Separatism and the Dismemberment of Territories (January – March 1918)
objects.description: Having been forced to recognize Ukraine's independence under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the government of Soviet Russia attempted to retain control over the eastern industrial regions. To this end, a separate separatist entity (the Donetsk–Kryvyi Rih Soviet Republic) was artificially constructed on the territory of the Donbas and the Kryvyi Rih region, with the aim of directly subordinating these lands to the central Russian authorities, bypassing the UNR(Citation: Україна й українці в постімперську добу (1917—1939) 2021)(Citation: Відносини держави, суспільства і особи під час створення радянського ладу в Україні (1917 – 1938 рр.) 2013).

objects.name: Soviet-Ukrainian War: Second Invasion and Resource Depletion (1919)
objects.description: After Germany's capitulation in World War I, the German and Austro-Hungarian troops that had occupied Ukraine since the spring of 1918 left(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003) - and in January 1919 RSFSR troops invaded Ukraine for the second time: the Soviet-Ukrainian War went on(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1 2003). The cover had been prepared in advance: as early as 28 November 1918, the Central Committee of the Bolshevik party (CC RCP(b)) created a "Provisional Workers' and Peasants' Government of Ukraine" in the Russian city of Kursk to provide political cover for the invasion(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 10 2013). The goal was the resources of the captured land: the head of the RSFSR government, Lenin, advised Petrograd workers to go to Ukraine for provisions and fuel - "It is foolish to starve and perish in Petrograd when you can win back bread and coal"(Citation: Петроградским организациям 1919). The villages answered the grain seizures with uprisings, and the Russian command treated the war against them as frontline work(Citation: Докладная записка В. А. Антонова-Овсеенко главкому 1919). In the summer of 1919 a second Russian army came to Ukraine - the Armed Forces of South Russia under General Denikin (the "Whites"), who likewise denied Ukrainian statehood(Citation: К населению Малороссии 1919). On 30 August 1919 Ukrainian troops took Kyiv, abandoned by the Bolsheviks, but on 31 August the Whites pushed them out - the day went down in history as the "Kyiv Catastrophe"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 4 2007). By the autumn of 1919 the Whites had driven out the RSFSR troops and established their military dictatorship over most of Ukraine(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 2 2004). In December 1919 Soviet Russia invaded for the third time (campaign C0104).

objects.name: Soviet-Ukrainian War: Third Invasion and the Final Soviet Occupation (December 1919 - November 1921)
objects.description: In December 1919, having defeated the White army of General Denikin, the troops of Soviet Russia (RSFSR) invaded Ukraine for the third time in two years of the Soviet-Ukrainian War: on 16 December they captured Kyiv - Soviet troops had previously taken it in February 1918 (campaign C0072) and in February 1919 (campaign C0074)(Citation: Відносини держави, суспільства і особи під час створення радянського ладу в Україні (1917 – 1938 рр.) 2013)(Citation: Директивы командования фронтов Красной армии (1917–1922). Т. 2 1972). The Army of the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR), no longer able to hold a continuous front, went on a raid behind the lines of the Soviet and White forces - the First Winter Campaign (6 December 1919 - 6 May 1920)(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011), while the UNR government concluded an alliance with Poland. In May 1920 Polish troops and the UNR Army liberated Kyiv, but on 12 June Soviet troops captured it again, and by autumn - most of the lands west of the Dnipro(Citation: Директивы командования фронтов Красной армии (1917–1922). Т. 3 1974). In November 1920 the UNR Army and government were pushed beyond the Zbruch River and retreated to territory under Polish control(Citation: Нариси історії Української революції 1917–1921 років: Кн. 2 2012). The last attempt by Ukrainians to raise an uprising against the Russian invaders was the Second Winter Campaign of the UNR Army: in November 1921 its detachments returned to Ukraine, were encircled, and 359 prisoners were executed near the village of Bazar(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 2 2004)(Citation: Вигнати окупанта 1963). Thus Soviet Russia, and from 1922 the USSR, entrenched itself on the captured lands of Ukraine until 1991(Citation: Відносини держави, суспільства і особи під час створення радянського ладу в Україні (1917 – 1938 рр.) 2013)(Citation: Україна й українці в постімперську добу (1917—1939) 2021).

objects.name: Legal Absorption through the Creation of the USSR (1922–1924)
objects.description: Formal consolidation of the seizure of Ukraine by dragging it into the so-called Union of SSRs. The unification of equal republics with the right of free secession was declared, but in practice the union treaty (December 1922) and the Constitution of the USSR (1924) became instruments of rigid centralization. objects.name: Forced Collectivization and Dekulakization (1928–1932)
objects.description: An assault on the traditional way of life of the Ukrainian village, which remained the principal bearer of national identity and economic independence. Peasants who put up resistance were dispossessed en masse and deported to Siberia and the North(Citation: Відносини держави, суспільства і особи під час створення радянського ладу в Україні (1917 – 1938 рр.) 2013).

objects.name: Annexation and Sovietization of Western Ukraine (1939–1941)
objects.description: The collusion of two totalitarian regimes (the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact), which led to the USSR's invasion of Poland and the seizure of Western Ukraine. Then came the mass deportations: "Between September 1939 and June 1941, up to 1,250,000 people (about 10% of the population) were removed from these lands and Western Belarus… to remote regions of the USSR"(Citation: Депортація (Енциклопедія Сучасної України) 2007).

objects.description: A return to total control over culture after the relative relaxations of the war years: the rout of the Ukrainian creative intelligentsia, accusations of "bourgeois nationalism" (attacks on Rylsky, Yanovsky, the persecution of Sosiura for the poem "Love Ukraine"). objects.name: Suppression of the GULAG Uprisings (1953–1954)
objects.description: After Stalin's death, the amnesty did not extend to political prisoners, among whom Ukrainians made up an enormous share. This provoked large-scale uprisings within the concentration camp system (Vorkuta, Norilsk, Kengir). In Kengir, the insurgents created a system of self-government, a radio station, and workshops for making weapons, demanding the arrival of a commission of the CPSU Central Committee. During the suppression of the Norilsk uprising, "about 100 people were killed and more than 200 wounded"(Citation: Норильский завет 2013). In Kengir, the authorities sent in the army: "1,600 soldiers, 3 fire engines, and 5 tanks moved into the zone. It was the only suppression of camp uprisings with tanks in Soviet history"(Citation: 70 років жорстокого придушення Кенгірського повстання 2024).

objects.name: The Ideological Campaign of the "300th Anniversary of Reunification" and the Transfer of Crimea (1954)
objects.description: A state propaganda operation: to mask Ukraine's colonial status, the empire celebrated with pomp the anniversary of the Pereiaslav Council, constructing the myth of a "single people." As part of the same campaign, Crimea was transferred to the Ukrainian SSR – the decree of the USSR Supreme Soviet Presidium of 19 February 1954 motivated it thus: "Taking into account the commonality of the economy, territorial proximity, and close economic and cultural ties between the Crimean oblast and the Ukrainian SSR"(Citation: Указ о передаче Крымской области из состава РСФСР в состав УССР 1954). The real context of the decision: "After the Second World War, the deportation of the Crimean Tatar people and mass resettlements from other regions of the USSR, the peninsula is in a deep socio-economic crisis," and "Moscow admits ever more openly: the Crimean region is a problem territory that the union center does not know how to sustain"(Citation: Подарунок Хрущова — Крим у складі Української РСР — що насправді відбулося у 1954 році (Суспільне) 2026).

objects.name: The First Wave of Repressions Against the "Sixtiers" (1965–1968)

objects.name: Stalling Democratic Reforms and Countering the People's Movement (Rukh) (1989–1990)
objects.description: The conservative party apparatus under the leadership of V. Shcherbytsky attempted to contain the growth of the national liberation movement. Because of KGB pressure and the threat of an immediate ban, the founders of the Ukrainian independence movement were initially forced to disguise their goals, naming the organization the "People's Movement of Ukraine for Perestroika": "at first it supported the official course of perestroika, without formally raising the demand of Ukraine's independence," and its program "lacked the demand for a new union treaty and contained a formal provision recognizing the 'guiding role' of the communist party"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 7 2010). Only in 1990, having proclaimed that "what is needed is not perestroika but the complete dismantling of the totalitarian system," did Rukh remove the words "for perestroika" from its name(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 7 2010).

objects.name: Manipulative Referendum on the Preservation of the USSR (March 1991)
objects.description: Moscow's attempt to legitimize the preservation of a disintegrating empire. The all-Union ballot contained the question: "Do you consider necessary the preservation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics as a renewed federation of equal sovereign republics in which the rights and freedoms of a person of any nationality will be fully guaranteed"(Citation: Постановление ВС СССР об организации референдума 1991). The Verkhovna Rada of the Ukrainian SSR added its own question – on Ukraine's membership in the Union "on the basis of the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Ukraine"(Citation: Постанова ВР УРСР про проведення референдуму 1991), which is what made the outcome ambiguous. The ambiguous wording was approved by the USSR Supreme Soviet in a resolution signed by its chairman Lukyanov(Citation: Постановление ВС СССР об организации референдума 1991).

objects.name: Attempted Coup d'État by the GKChP (August 1991)
objects.description: An armed mutiny by the conservative wing of the Soviet leadership, the KGB, and the army aimed at halting the USSR's disintegration and holding the republics by force. objects.name: Gas Wars and Energy Blackmail (2006–2009)
objects.description: The use of the state monopoly Gazprom as a political weapon against Kyiv's independent course. Gas supplies were cut off at the height of winter: "at 10.00am Moscow time on January 1, 2006, Gazprom cut off gas supplies to Ukraine"(Citation: The Russian-Ukrainian gas crisis of January 2006 2006), and three years later "Russian exports to Ukraine were cut off on 1 January. Exports to 16 EU member states and Moldova were drastically reduced on 6 January and cut completely from 7 January"(Citation: The Russo-Ukrainian gas dispute of January 2009 2009). Supplies ran through opaque intermediaries (RosUkrEnergo), whose use "was long criticized in European government circles and by corporate governance bodies"(Citation: The Russo-Ukrainian gas dispute of January 2009 2009), while RUE's co-owner Dmytro Firtash admitted to the US ambassador that "he needed Mogilevich's approval to get into business in the first place"(Citation: Cable 08KYIV2414: Firtash makes his case to the USG 2008).

objects.name: Diplomatic Attack Against NATO Enlargement (2008)
objects.description: Diplomatic blackmail by V. Putin around the NATO summit in Bucharest aimed at blocking the granting of a Membership Action Plan (MAP) to Ukraine. Two days after the summit, at a meeting with G. Bush in Sochi, the Russian leader denied Ukrainian statehood - Ukraine, in his words, "is not a nation built in a natural manner" but "an artificial country created back in Soviet times"(Citation: Memorandum of Conversation: Meeting with President of Russia (Sochi) 2008) - and directly threatened its rupture: "the country could just split apart," adding that, relying on anti-NATO forces, "Russia would be creating problems there all the time"(Citation: Memorandum of Conversation: Meeting with President of Russia (Sochi) 2008). At the summit itself, as retold by Kommersant's source, Putin told Bush: "You understand, George, that Ukraine is not even a state!" - in effect threatening "that Russia could begin the severance of Crimea and Eastern Ukraine"(Citation: Блок НАТО разошелся на блокпакеты (Коммерсантъ) 2008).

objects.name: Derailing the Association with the EU (2013–2014)
objects.description: Economic and political pressure by V. Putin on V. Yanukovych in the autumn of 2013 aimed at derailing the signing of the Association Agreement with the EU. The price was formalized publicly on December 17, 2013: "Ukraine will receive 15 billion dollars from Russia and gas at a reduced price" - the gas price was lowered "to 268.5 dollars per thousand cubic meters" instead of the previous 410, and the money came "from the Russian National Welfare Fund" in exchange for Ukrainian government securities(Citation: Виктор Янукович и Владимир Путин достигли компромисса в Москве 2013). The refusal to sign the agreement triggered the protests: "between 21 November 2013 and 22 February 2014 large-scale street protests took place, provoked by the decision of then-President Viktor Yanukovych not to sign the association agreement with the European Union," and their suppression ended in shootings - on the Maidan "between January and February 2014 more than 100 people were killed, including by snipers"(Citation: Доклад Верховного комиссара ООН по правам человека о положении в области прав человека в Украине (A/HRC/27/75) 2014).

objects.name: Continuation of the Russo-Ukrainian War: Armed Aggression in the Donbas (2014–2015)
